title: Letting the story change
hookLine: the story of the hurt can change as you do

cards: Every hurt comes with a story, and the story gets told. To a friend the week it happens, hot and fast. To a partner a year later, with a sigh.
To yourself in the car, in the same words every time, like a song on repeat. The facts in those stories don't change; what happened, happened. But the telling can change, because the teller does.
The book of Ruth has a woman whose story is told one way in its first chapter and another way in its last. Today: letting the story change.

teach.b: First, the first telling. Naomi has buried her husband and both her sons in a foreign country. When she comes home to Bethlehem, the women of the town ask, is this Naomi?
She answers, in the King James words: "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter.
She renames herself after the hurt. Second, that telling was true.
She goes on: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." The book doesn't correct her. Nobody tells her to look on the bright side.
The bitter telling gets its full say, and it stays in the book. Third, the second telling. By the last chapter a lot has happened: Ruth's loyalty, a harvest, a marriage, a baby.
And the women of the town tell the story again: "There is a son born to Naomi."

teach.h: THE SAME FACTS, A LIVING TELLER.
teach.b: Naomi, not Mara. The graves from chapter one are still there. What changed is that the story kept going, and so did she.
Fourth, a test for a new telling. Is it still true? Does it still name the loss, or the wrong, plainly?
And does it have room for who you are now, not only who you were the day it happened? A new telling isn't a happier lie. It's the same facts, told by someone who has kept living.

how: Jews read the book of Ruth on the festival of Shavuot, and Christians read it among the books of the Old Testament.

o: Ruth's new name after she married in Bethlehem
the name Naomi took in her grief; it means bitter
the hometown Naomi returned to after her losses

s: in Ruth, someone tells Naomi to stop being bitter
the book lets her bitter telling stand: "call me Mara."
by the last chapter, the women speak of Naomi by her own name again
"there is a son born to Naomi."
a new telling means inventing a happier version
the facts stay exactly; the teller has changed.

games.q: you're Naomi, home in Bethlehem after burying your husband and your sons. the women of the town ask, is this Naomi? what do you say?
o: call me Mara: I went out full and came home empty.
games.why: she renames herself bitter, and the book lets it stand. by the last chapter the same town tells her story again, with her own name in it.

practice: Choose one hurt you've told many times, and hear the usual telling once, in its usual words.

Now tell it again silently, keeping the facts exactly and naming the wrong plainly, but add one sentence about what came after, something you did, learned or survived; if there's no after yet, the sentence can be: and I'm still here.
Let the new telling sit without forcing a happy ending, and if you pray, you can offer both versions in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Mara. The name Naomi gave herself after her losses, bitter, before the story was told again at the book's end. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Ruth 1:20: bitter, the name Naomi gives herself.

carryVoice: Your line: a new telling. Naomi's story didn't stop at Mara. That's day nine hundred ninety-one.
